items.statement: Let $F$ be a compact connected surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, and let $\gamma\subset\operatorname{int}F$ be an embedded circle with a supplied orientation. Supply a finite triangular presentation of $F$ in which $\partial F$ and $\gamma$ are subcomplexes. If $[\gamma]=0$ in $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, then $\gamma$ separates $F$ and is the entire boundary of a compact connected orientable subsurface $A\subset\operatorname{int}F$. Its orientation can be chosen to induce the supplied orientation of $\gamma$. The inclusion $H_1(A;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is injective. The assertion is choice-free for the supplied finite presentation.

citations.quote:
For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

derivations.claim: By [F1] there is a rational simplicial two-chain $c$ whose boundary is the oriented edge cycle $\gamma$. Give the finitely many triangles arbitrary reference orientations and record their coefficients in $c$. Across every interior edge not in $\gamma$, the two triangle coefficients have equal absolute value, since their signed boundary coefficients cancel. Wherever that absolute value is nonzero, the coefficient signs give coherent orientations of the incident triangles. A boundary edge of $F$ is incident to one triangle and does not occur in $\partial c$, so that triangle has coefficient zero.

The triangles on each connected component of $F\setminus\gamma$ are joined by adjacencies across edges not in $\gamma$: a path between interior points can be moved off the finitely many vertices and made transverse to the finitely many edges, yielding such a finite edge path. Thus the absolute coefficients are constant on each component. Every component that meets $\partial F$ has coefficient zero by step 1.1. There is at least one such component, because $\partial F$ is nonempty.

There are at most two components of $F\setminus\gamma$. Indeed a small interval on $\gamma$ has two local sides; following them once around the connected circle either retains two sides or exchanges them. A sufficiently small regular neighborhood therefore has at most two components after its central circle is deleted. Every complementary component meets this neighborhood, since otherwise it would be both open and closed in connected $F$; and each connected side of the neighborhood belongs to one complementary component. If there were only one component, step 2.1 would make every coefficient zero, contradicting $\partial c=\gamma$. Hence there are exactly two, one of them with zero coefficients and containing $\partial F$. Across each edge of $\gamma$ the jump is one, so the other component has coefficient absolute value one and does not meet $\partial F$. Let $A$ be its closure. The local two-side charts show that $A$ is a compact connected subsurface with boundary exactly $\gamma$. The coherent orientations in step 1.1 orient $A$ so that its oriented fundamental two-chain has boundary $\gamma$. Thus $A\subset\operatorname{int}F$ is the required orientable side.

Let a rational simplicial one-cycle $z$ in $A$ become zero in $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. By [F1] choose a rational two-chain $d$ in $F$ with $\partial d=z$. On the other complementary component, all interior-edge coefficients of $\partial d$ vanish because $z$ is supported in $A$, and its edges on $\partial F$ also have coefficient zero. The same propagation as in steps 1.1–2.1 forces every triangle coefficient of $d$ on that component to be zero. Therefore $d$ is supported in $A$, so $z$ already bounds there. Every homology class of $A$ has such a simplicial representative by [F1]. This proves the asserted injection.

Steps 3.1–4.1 give the orientable one-boundary subsurface and its homology injection. In particular a one-sided circle cannot meet the nullhomology hypothesis: its two local sides are exchanged, so the complement in step 3.1 would be connected. The argument also allows $A$ to be a disk and uses only finitely many coefficients, triangle adjacencies and reference orientations. No orientation of the original surface and no choice principle were assumed.

items.statement: Assume full AC. Let $F_+,F_-$ be connected compact smooth surfaces embedded in the oriented standard three-sphere, each with nonempty boundary and possibly nonorientable. Supply quadratic forms $q_\pm$ on $H_1(F_\pm;\mathbb Q)$, positive definite and negative definite respectively. Suppose that for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ in the interior of the corresponding surface, $q_\pm[c]=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau_\pm c)$. Here $\tau_\pm c$ is the cycle obtained by pushing the two-sheeted unit normal line cover of $c$ a sufficiently small distance off that surface, with both sheets oriented by projection to $c$; linking is extended bilinearly over rational coefficients. Let $\gamma$ be a smooth embedded circle in both interiors, and assume their tangent planes are transverse along $\gamma$. Then $\gamma$ bounds a smooth embedded disk in each of $F_+$ and $F_-$. Zero-dimensional first homology is allowed in the definiteness assumptions. The statement makes no assertion that the two disk interiors are mutually disjoint.

citations.quote:
In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a compact codimension-zero $C^2$ subsurface of a Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless $C^2$ surface $S$, with $C^2$ boundary. Let $G\subset\operatorname{Int}N$ be a finite embedded graph: its vertices are distinct points, each edge is a regular $C^2$ embedded arc up to its endpoints, and different edge interiors are disjoint and avoid the vertices. Closed regular edges may first be subdivided by inserting finitely many vertices. Then $N$ has a finite triangular cellulation containing $G\cup\partial N$ in its one-skeleton. Each closed triangle is an embedded topological disk, the prescribed graph and original boundary retain their regular $C^2$ arcs, and the cell maps induce a homeomorphism from a finite abstract simplicial complex onto $N$ after finite subdivision. Interior edges have two incident triangles and boundary edges one; vertex links are circles or intervals, respectively.

A cell map is required to be a homeomorphism; the statement does not assert a differentiable straightening of an arbitrary prescribed graph at its vertices. This permits tangencies between prescribed edge germs. The empty $N$ or empty $G$ is allowed.

Let $F$ be a compact connected surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, and let $\gamma\subset\operatorname{int}F$ be an embedded circle with a supplied orientation. Supply a finite triangular presentation of $F$ in which $\partial F$ and $\gamma$ are subcomplexes. If $[\gamma]=0$ in $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, then $\gamma$ separates $F$ and is the entire boundary of a compact connected orientable subsurface $A\subset\operatorname{int}F$. Its orientation can be chosen to induce the supplied orientation of $\gamma$. The inclusion $H_1(A;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ is injective. The assertion is choice-free for the supplied finite presentation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, and let $F,F'$ be any connected compact smooth oriented spanning surfaces for $K$. For any ordered integral bases of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, the matrices of the positive-push Seifert pairing are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two rank-two elementary Seifert enlargements or their reverses.

Assume full AC. For every $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$, changing an ordered basis by an integral unimodular congruence or changing a knot Seifert matrix by either elementary enlargement or reduction preserves the signature of $H_\omega$. Consequently, the nonroot Levine–Tristram signature and its one-sided-average value at every Alexander root are independent of the spanning surface and basis.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] to collar the boundaries of both surfaces. Gluing two copies by reflection in the boundary collar gives for each a compact smooth boundaryless double; the collar charts have signed normal coordinate, so each original surface is a codimension-zero smooth subsurface of its double. The double is Hausdorff and second-countable, as follows from the two finite compact chart covers and the finitely many collar charts. Subdivide $\gamma$ by finitely many vertices and apply [F2]. This supplies a finite triangular presentation of each $F_\pm$ relative to its boundary and $\gamma$. No orientability of the doubles is required.

Orient $\gamma$ arbitrarily and use the round metric of $S^3$. Its normal planes are oriented by its tangent and the ambient orientation. The two surface normal lines $n_+(s),n_-(s)$ are distinct lines in these planes by transversality. There is a unique positively oriented angle $\theta(s)\in(0,\pi)$ carrying the first unoriented line to the second. This is a smooth function on the circle, including when either normal line bundle is nontrivial: line angles are taken modulo $\pi$, and their nonzero difference has a unique representative in that open interval. For a sufficiently small constant radius, rotate both unit vectors of $n_+(s)$ through $t\theta(s)$ in their normal plane. These are embedded cycles disjoint from $\gamma$, varying by an isotopy and ending at the two normal pushes for $F_-$. To verify the needed tube directly, the round exponential map from the normal plane bundle has invertible differential on its zero section by [F7]; compactness gives a common small radius, and collisions at arbitrarily small radii would converge to one base point, contradicting that local inverse. Both possible connectedness types of the two-sheeted normal cover are therefore included. The cycles retain their orientation by projection to $\gamma$. Their linking with $\gamma$ is unchanged, since this isotopy is a homology in its complement. Thus $q_+[\gamma]=\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,\tau_+\gamma)=\operatorname{lk}(\gamma,\tau_-\gamma)=q_-[\gamma]$.

Positive definiteness makes the first value nonnegative and zero only at the zero class. Negative definiteness makes the last nonpositive and zero only at the zero class. Their equality in step 1.2 forces both to be zero and forces $[\gamma]=0$ in each rational homology group. Apply [F3] in the presentations from step 1.1 to obtain orientable connected subsurfaces $A_\pm$ with sole boundary $\gamma$ and injective homology maps into $F_\pm$. The subsurfaces have the inherited smooth structure: near $\gamma$ their boundary is one smooth side of that interior circle, and elsewhere their points are interior points of $F_\pm$. Orient both so that their boundary orientation is the same chosen orientation of $\gamma$.

The restricted forms on $H_1(A_\pm;\mathbb Q)$ remain respectively positive and negative definite by the injections in step 2.1. Let $V_\pm$ be positive-push Seifert matrices for these two oriented spanning surfaces of the actual knot $\gamma$. Their symmetrizations give precisely those restrictions. Indeed on an oriented multicurve $c\subset A_\pm$, its two normal sheets are $c^++c^-$. Moving the disjoint pair $(c^-,c)$ together through the normal collar to $(c,c^+)$ preserves linking, while symmetry in [F4] gives $\operatorname{lk}(c,c^-)=\operatorname{lk}(c,c^+)$. Hence $q_\pm[c]=2\operatorname{lk}(c^+,c)=c^T(V_\pm+V_\pm^T)c$. All integral classes have multicurve representatives by [F4]; multiplying by a denominator handles rational classes. Equality of the quadratic forms on all those classes gives equality of the associated symmetric forms by polarization. The normal collar on $A_\pm$ is the restriction of the ambient normal collar on $F_\pm$, so no framing change occurs.

By [F5] the two Seifert matrices are S-equivalent. Apply [F6] at $\omega=-1$, where $H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)$, to conclude that their symmetrizations have the same signature; positive multiplication by two does not change positive or negative indices. Write $r_\pm=\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_1(A_\pm;\mathbb Q)$. By step 3.1 their signatures are $r_+$ and $-r_-$, including dimension zero. Therefore $r_+=-r_-$, and since both are nonnegative integers, both vanish. This uses the proved knot S-equivalence and ordinary signature calculation, without a Gordon–Litherland signature formula.

For completeness the zero homology conclusion makes each $A_\pm$ a disk by a finite collapse argument. In its finite triangulation choose a spanning tree in the triangle adjacency graph with an additional exterior vertex joined along boundary edges. This graph is connected by the surface vertex links and connectedness. Starting at the exterior, delete each triangle together with its edge toward its already deleted parent; that edge is free at its deletion. A free-side triangle collapses onto its two other sides. The remaining connected finite graph is a spine. The original surface is homeomorphic to a thickening of this graph: reversing one collapse attaches a triangular disk bulge along the two retained side intervals, which is a disk replacement relative to those intervals, and reversing the finite list recovers the surface thickening. A connected finite graph has first rational homology of dimension its number of edges outside a spanning tree, by its edge boundary matrix. Step 4.1 thus makes this graph a tree. A thickening of a tree is a disk, by removing leaf disks and their incident bands until one vertex disk remains. Consequently each $A_\pm$ is a disk region with its smooth inherited surface structure and smooth boundary $\gamma$, proving the assertion. The two disks need not have disjoint interiors, and none has been asserted.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Since $P$ is real, $H_\omega(P^TVP)=P^TH_\omega(V)P$. An invertible congruence is a change of coordinates in the associated Hermitian form, so its positive and negative indices are unchanged: a maximal positive subspace maps bijectively by $P$, and likewise for negative subspaces. Hence the signature is invariant under basis change. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Put $c=1-\omega\ne0$. For either enlargement, the enlarged Hermitian matrix has block form
$$\widetilde H=\begin{pmatrix}H&b&0\\b^*&z(c+\bar c)&\lambda\\0&\bar\lambda&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad |\lambda|=|c|>0,$$
where $H=H_\omega(V)$, $b$ is the column determined by the enlargement vectors, and $z\in\mathbb Z$. The lower $2\times2$ block $D$ has determinant $-|c|^2<0$, hence one positive and one negative eigenvalue. Its inverse has $(D^{-1})_{11}=0$. The block congruence eliminating $b$ therefore has Schur complement $H-b(D^{-1})_{11}b^*=H$, so $\widetilde H$ is congruent to $H\oplus D$. The block $D$ contributes signature $0$, proving enlargement invariance for every $\omega\ne1$, including singular parameters. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], any two knot matrices are connected by the operations of steps 1.1 and 2.1, so their signatures agree at every nonroot parameter. The one-sided signatures are equal as functions on each punctured neighboring arc; by [F3] their arithmetic averages are defined and agree at a root as well. Reductions reverse the same equalities. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
